issues.legal_issue: A landlord who carries on business in a non-residential building of which the landlord is a co-owner occupies a building of the landlord’s own for the purpose of the business-need ground for eviction.
material_facts: The eviction petition was based on the landlord’s claim that he carried on business in rented premises and did not occupy a building of his own for that business.
During the appeal, the landlord died and his heirs became co-owners of the rented premises from which eviction was sought.
The active partners carrying on the business occupied another non-residential building of which they were co-owners.
issues.conclusion: The co-owned business premises counted as the landlords’ own building, so they were not entitled to retain eviction on the ground that they did not occupy a building of their own for the business.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the relevant building need not be solely owned by the landlord: a co-owner is an owner of the property. The Court relied on Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, which held that a co-owner is as much an owner of the entire property as a sole owner.

predicates.nonresidential_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction from a non-residential building.
predicates.business_need_ground_asserted: The landlord seeks the building for a business on the basis that the landlord does not occupy a building of their own for that business.
predicates.landlord_carries_business_in_coowned_bui: The landlord carries on the relevant business in a building of which the landlord is a co-owner.

issues.definition: When a non-residential eviction proceeding relies on a business need and the landlord carries on that business in a co-owned building, the landlord is treated as occupying their own business premises and is disentitled to eviction on the stated ground.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing a pending appeal against an eviction order may consider material developments that occurred after the eviction proceeding began and may alter the relief accordingly, even though the order was affirmed below.
material_facts: The tenant’s appeal by special leave was pending when the original landlord died and the business was shifted to a different building.
The landlord’s heirs became co-owners of both the building where the business was being carried on and the building from which eviction had been ordered.
The subsequent ownership and business arrangements affected whether the landlords remained entitled to eviction, and the eviction order had not become final while the appeal was pending.
issues.conclusion: The Court could consider the subsequent developments in the pending appeal and set aside the eviction order; the order did not give the landlords an indefeasible vested right before becoming final and conclusive.
issues.legal_principle: A mere right to take advantage of a statutory provision is not an accrued right, as stated in Abbott v. Minister for Lands and accepted in Kanaya Ram v. Rajender Kumar. Under Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders, a court may, subject to fairness and any contrary legal or equitable circumstances, take cautious notice of post-filing events that fundamentally affect entitlement to relief or how relief should be moulded. That power applies in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_order_pending: A party has a pending appeal against an eviction order.
predicates.material_post_filing_change_affects_enti: A development after the proceeding began materially changes a fact bearing on entitlement to relief or the form of relief.
predicates.eviction_order_not_final: The eviction order remains under challenge and has not become final and conclusive.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal remains pending, a later development materially affects entitlement, and the eviction order is not final, the court may consider that development and mould the relief.
